newsitem.title: UK: Regan isolated as former CWS bid allies desert him.
newsitem.headline: Regan isolated as former CWS bid allies desert him.

text.p: Young entrepreneur Andrew Regan looked increasingly isolated on Monday as British merchant bank Hambros, a key ally in his failed bid for Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), withdrew as adviser to his companies.
"Hambros is today retiring as financial advisers to Galileo and Lanica Trust," Hambros said in a statement.
Hambros settled with the CWS and apologised for its part in the bid while City law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite, which also advised Galileo and Lanica, also settled.

Regan, the 31-year-old behind the discredited 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) takeover plan, has been incommunicado since Galileo admitted defeat in the face of CWS legal action and the withdrawal of a key backer.

The publicity-shy Regan has remained a mystery man throughout, keeping his public involvement to a minimum since plans to mount a takeover of the CWS emerged in February, while remaining in the thick of it behind the scenes.

His stance has been almost entirely put forward by public relations firms, with details of the bid emerging piecemeal over the past few months, with a rapid acceleration in the week immediately before it was expected to emerge.

In the event the takeover was scotched by a High Court injunction granted to the CWS preventing the use of confidential information leaked to Regan, his business associate David Lyons, his Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica and its offshoot Galileo.

Allan Green, the senior CWS executive who has admitted to passing on the highly sensitive papers, was sacked at the weekend following his suspension a week earlier. David Chambers, another CWS manager was also sacked.

As a result of receiving these documents, which Lyons said were passed on voluntarily, Lyons and Regan now not only face paying CWS costs but also a private prosecution, with a preliminary hearing due to take place in the City of London magistrates court on May 28.

Regan is not expected to make any statements about the affair "until the legal situation has become clearer", one banking source said, adding that the father of five felt "rather let down by his advisers".
"Someone should have told him if there was something so massively wrong," the source added.
With Hambros now out of the frame in terms of legal action, the CWS will have more time and energy to devote to pursuing Regan and his immediate business partners.

Last week CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth said he would be failing in his duty to the hundreds of thousands of members of the supermarkets to funeral parlours group if he simply stopped at defeating the bid.
"I have an obligation to the members to pursue this matter to the end," he said.
CWS has interests ranging from travel agents and farms to the profitable Co-operative Bank and insurance giant Co-operative Insurance Society (CIS).

The mutually-owned group traces its roots back to the Rochdale Pioneers who banded together in Lancashire, north west England in 1844 and its battle against Regan and his plan to offer its members cash was portrayed as a fight between opposing cultures.
In fact CWS has done business with Regan before and it was this which led in part to his break-up plan being discredited.

Regan was chief executive of a company called Hobson which in 1994 bought the CWS food manufacturing group. A supply agreement between the two was extended in January 1995 after negotiations between Regan and the former CWS managers Green and Chambers.

During the course of its defence, CWS raised doubts about a 2.4 million pound payment to a third party called Trellis International. Regan has stated the money was paid by Hobson to Ronald Zimet at Trellis for "assisting with and conducting negotiations with CWS".

But the CWS was not happy with the answers it received from Regan and last week it passed on its concerns to Britain's Serious Fraud Office, which on Monday repeated that it is not investigating the affair.
Sources say that Regan must get Zimet, who is widely reported to live in Israel, to come forward and back up his explanation of the deal if he is to restore his credibility.

Regan's other main hurdle if he wishes to regain the confidence of the City, which he will need if he is to be involved in any future deals, will be to explain his part in the outflow of confidential CWS information. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
